explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Malachi asks, "Why then do we break faith with one another so as to profane the covenant of our fathers?" (Malachi 2:10). He says "we," so he counts himself in. The question is plain: same Father, same God, so why treat each other like that?

Grudges are a human thing, but Malachi doesn't name them here. He asks why "…we break faith with one another…" (Malachi 2:10). Breaking faith means not keeping your word to someone. The question comes right after "Do we not all have one Father?"

Rumors get around fast, but they're not named in this verse. Malachi asks, "Why then do we break faith with one another…" (Malachi 2:10). The words he uses are "break faith," and that's the answer here. The question comes right after "Do we not all have one Father?"

explanations.answer: By marrying the daughter of a foreign god
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says Judah profaned the LORD's beloved sanctuary "…by marrying the daughter of a foreign god." (Malachi 2:11). Malachi calls it an abomination and says it happened in Israel and in Jerusalem. That's how seriously he says it.

explanations.answer: By bowing down to the idol of a foreign god
explanations.explanation: Bowing to an idol sounds like a good guess, but that's not what Malachi says. The verse says Judah profaned the sanctuary "…by marrying the daughter of a foreign god." (Malachi 2:11). Marriage is the act named here. Stick to what the verse says and you'll stay out of the doughy zone.

explanations.answer: By burning incense to the image of a foreign god
explanations.explanation: Incense is a fine guess, but it's not in this verse. Malachi says Judah profaned the LORD's beloved sanctuary "…by marrying the daughter of a foreign god." (Malachi 2:11). No incense, no image. Just the marriage, and he calls it an abomination.

I see why you'd lean that way, friend, but it's False. Malachi says the LORD may cut off from the tents of Jacob everyone who is awake and aware, "…even if he brings an offering to the LORD of Hosts." (Malachi 2:12). The offering doesn't cover it. Bringing a box of cookies doesn't make up for breaking your word.

That's right, it's False. Malachi says, "…may the LORD cut off from the tents of Jacob everyone who is awake and aware—even if he brings an offering to the LORD of Hosts." (Malachi 2:12). So no, the man is not safe. The offering doesn't change that.

explanations.answer: The LORD no longer receives their offerings gladly
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. Malachi says they cover the altar with tears "…because He no longer regards your offerings or receives them gladly from your hands." (Malachi 2:13). The weeping is real. The text gives that reason and no other.

explanations.answer: Their enemies have broken down the city walls
explanations.explanation: Walls coming down would be rough, but the text doesn't say that. The people weep "…because He no longer regards your offerings or receives them gladly from your hands." (Malachi 2:13). The trouble is at the altar. No enemies show up in this verse.

explanations.answer: The rain has stopped falling on their fields
explanations.explanation: No rain talk in this verse, friend. Malachi says they cover the altar with tears "…because He no longer regards your offerings or receives them gladly from your hands." (Malachi 2:13). The reason is about the offerings. Fields and weather don't come up.

True! The people ask "Why?" and Malachi answers, "It is because the LORD has been a witness between you and the wife of your youth…" (Malachi 2:14). The LORD is the witness between a man and his wife. I think that's a heavy thing to hear, and Malachi says it straight.

It's actually True. Malachi says, "It is because the LORD has been a witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have broken faith…" (Malachi 2:14). That's his answer to their "Why?" The LORD has been a witness between the man and his wife. I think this one lands hard.
Yes, companion! Malachi says she is "…your companion and your wife by covenant." (Malachi 2:14). A companion is someone who walks beside you. She's named that way right alongside the covenant.
Not servant, friend. The verse says she is "…your companion and your wife by covenant." (Malachi 2:14). A companion is a partner at your side. Nothing in the line makes her a servant.

Neighbor is a good word, but it's not the one here. Malachi says she is "…your companion and your wife by covenant." (Malachi 2:14). She's named as a companion and a wife, not a neighbor. Even I'd say that's a bigger deal than lending someone a cup of flour.
Godly it is, baker! Malachi asks, "And why one?" and answers, "Because He seeks godly offspring." (Malachi 2:15). That's the reason the text gives. Short answer, big meaning.

Wealthy doesn't make the list. Malachi says, "Because He seeks godly offspring." (Malachi 2:15). The word in that verse is godly, not wealthy. That's the reason the text gives for why the LORD made them one.
Fame is not in this verse, friend. Malachi says, "Because He seeks godly offspring." (Malachi 2:15). That's the reason he gives for why the LORD made them one. Godly, not famous.
